title: Why the U.S. Intervened to Prop Up Japan’s Yen | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: On Friday July 31, 2026 the U.S. Treasury sold euros from its reserves to buy yen alongside Japan — the first U.S. intervention to support the yen since 1998 — weeks after the yen hit a forty-year low. Setser argues the yen has overshot fundamentals that are actually stronger than America's on several metrics, that broad Asian currency weakness was working directly against the administration's reindustrialization goal, and that the durable fix is Bank of Japan rate hikes plus a shift in Japanese investors' currently unhedged foreign-asset positions.

themes.theme: The intervention mechanics and their rarity

insights.claim: The U.S. Treasury intervened on Friday July 31, 2026 by selling euros from its international reserves to buy Japanese yen — notably not by selling dollars — with Bessent confirming the operation on Monday August 3.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Funding intervention out of euro reserves caps its size at the reserve stock and is a signal Washington will not deliberately weaken the dollar — limits how far this can be scaled.
insights.quote: The United States intervened in currency markets this past Friday, July 31, selling euros from its international reserves and buying the Japanese yen.
insights.locator: The United States intervened in currency markets

insights.claim: U.S. intervention in support of the yen is exceptionally rare: the last such action was in 1998 during the Asian financial crisis, and the 2011 post-Fukushima operation ran the opposite direction, to keep the yen from rising rather than from falling.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: A once-in-28-year policy tool being deployed without a crisis backdrop marks a regime change in Treasury's willingness to manage cross rates.
insights.quote: The United States last intervened to support the yen in 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, so this is the first action in over twenty years to support the yen.
insights.locator: How common is it for the United States to do this

insights.claim: The article's own framing contains a discrepancy worth noting: the introduction describes the move as the first U.S. currency intervention for Japan since 2011, while Setser clarifies the last yen-supporting intervention was 1998 and the 2011 action was directionally opposite.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Precision matters for the precedent set: this is the first non-crisis, yen-supporting joint action in nearly three decades, a materially stronger signal than a 2011 comparison implies.
insights.quote: The coordinated effort marked the first time the United States has staged a currency intervention for Japan since 2011, and it came weeks after the yen hit a forty-year low last month.
insights.locator: The yen spiked against the dollar following the announcement

insights.claim: Bessent explicitly framed intervention as a signaling device that requires Japanese follow-through, saying intervention can send a market signal but Japan also needs to deliver policies that support the currency.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Treasury has pre-committed to conditionality — absent BoJ hikes, the intervention put has a short expiry and yen shorts get another window.
insights.quote: “A stable yen is not only important for the U.S., but very important for the entire region,” Bessent said.
insights.locator: Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent confirmed the details

themes.theme: Why Washington cared: the reindustrialization channel

insights.claim: A weak yen pressures other Asian currencies and makes it harder for China to keep allowing slow renminbi appreciation, so yen weakness propagates into a broad Asian competitiveness shift rather than staying a bilateral issue.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Trade yen weakness as a proxy for the whole Asian FX complex; a durable yen floor is the precondition for any CNY appreciation path.
insights.quote: A weak yen tends to put pressure on other Asian currencies, and it could make it harder for China to continue to allow a slow appreciation of its currency.
insights.locator: The main benefit of this operation

insights.claim: Broad Asian currency weakness was directly undermining the Trump administration's reindustrialization agenda because the currency market was signaling to invest in high-surplus Asia rather than in the United States.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: This reframes FX intervention as industrial policy — expect Treasury to treat exchange rates as a lever on manufacturing capex, raising the odds of repeat action.
insights.quote: The currency market was saying, “Invest more in high surplus Asia,” not “invest more in the United States.”
insights.locator: All these currencies are very weak

insights.claim: The primary immediate payoff of the operation is buying time — it stops, at least for a while, the risk of a disruptive further depreciation of the yen rather than reversing the trend.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Positioning for a sustained yen rally on intervention alone is premature; the author frames the benefit as tail-risk suppression, not trend reversal.
insights.locator: The main benefit of this operation

insights.claim: Trump publicly personalized the operation as alliance maintenance, telling reporters on Air Force One on Sunday August 2 that the United States is always there for Japan.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Presidential ownership of the intervention lowers the political barrier to repeating it, which matters for sizing the implicit yen put.
insights.quote: “We’re always there for Japan,” U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Air Force One on Sunday, August 2.
insights.locator: The coordinated effort marked the first time

themes.theme: Japan's fundamentals are stronger than the narrative

insights.claim: There is too much negativity around Japan's economy: it runs a substantial current account surplus as a share of GDP, the government holds a large stock of external assets, net government debt is trending down relative to GDP, and the headline fiscal deficit is around 1 percent of GDP.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: If Japan's fiscal and external metrics are improving, JGB and yen bearishness rests on rate differentials alone — which policy can change quickly.
insights.quote: There is a bit too much negativity around Japan’s economy right now tied the yen’s weakness.
insights.locator: What needs to happen next to sustain the yen

insights.claim: Japan's cabinet office has indicated the country will run a primary fiscal surplus this year, meaning taxes will cover noninterest spending — a position that on these indicators makes the Japanese economy look much better than that of the United States.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: A primary surplus in Japan against U.S. deficits is the strongest argument for structural yen upside once the carry incentive fades.
insights.quote: On these indicators the Japanese economy looks much better than that of the United States.

insights.claim: The inflation-adjusted yen is back to the low levels of the 1960s despite Japan being in a completely different economic position than during the Vietnam war era — an explicit valuation call that the currency has overshot.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: A sixty-year real-exchange-rate low with improving fundamentals frames long yen as a value trade with a policy catalyst attached.
insights.quote: The inflation-adjusted yen is back to the low levels of the 1960s.
insights.locator: What is the strategic benefit of propping up the yen?

insights.claim: The main requirement to support the yen is higher Bank of Japan policy rates, since Japanese short-term rates sit below U.S. rates and, more importantly, below the pace of Japanese inflation.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: Negative real short rates are the core driver — watch BoJ meetings, not MoF intervention headlines, for the durable turn in USDJPY.
insights.quote: The main thing Japan needs to support the yen is higher policy rates from the Bank of Japan.
insights.locator: The main thing Japan needs to support the yen

insights.claim: The durable stabilization recipe is two-part: reestablishing a credible intervention threat combined with a series of Bank of Japan rate hikes, not either alone.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: A reusable template for judging FX defenses: credibility plus rate policy. Intervention without hikes fails; the July 31 action only supplies half the formula.
insights.quote: Ultimately, reestablishing a credible intervention threat and a series of rate hikes should stabilize the yen.
insights.locator: Ultimately, reestablishing a credible intervention threat

insights.claim: Japanese investors have convinced themselves they do not need to pay the cost of hedging their large foreign assets, so any shift toward higher hedge ratios would generate substantial underlying market support for the yen.
insights.speaker: Brad W. Setser
insights.so_what: The unhedged foreign-asset stock is the largest latent yen bid in the system — a hedging-ratio inflection is a bigger and more lasting flow than any Treasury operation.
insights.quote: any change that leads to an increase in hedging would generate substantial underlying market support for the yen
